strengths: Combines GMsFEM multiscale basis construction with neural operators by training NOs to predict local subspaces rather than individual basis functions, targeting high-contrast multiscale PDEs.
Introduces subspace alignment losses (SAL and SAL-PR) that enforce geometric subspace consistency and empirically improve over the sign-invariant per-basis L2 loss in the reported experiments.
Reports substantial offline basis-generation speedups (~50-60x) over classical GMsFEM while maintaining comparable or slightly better L2/H1 accuracy on two benchmark PDE families.

Demonstrates independence from the forcing term: after training on one right-hand side, the method can be applied to a different forcing term, whereas a standalone NO fails catastrophically out of distribution.
Provides detailed training hyperparameters, architectures, and optimizer settings in the appendix, which supports partial reproducibility.
Explicitly discusses limitations, including restriction to structured grids, relatively small grid sizes, and time-independent PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: ML-assisted GMsFEM and learning multiscale basis functions have been explored before, and the closest prior work (Spiridonov et al., 2025) already predicts basis functions. The subspace loss is a natural extension of subspace-alignment/Procrustes objectives and lacks deeper theoretical or architectural novelty.

Evaluation is narrow: only two-dimensional structured grids, 100x100 fine resolution, 5x5 coarse grids, two PDE types, a single high-contrast coefficient family, 200 test samples, and Dirichlet boundary conditions. There is no 3D, irregular-domain, time-dependent, or real-world multiscale evaluation.

Computational comparison is incomplete: the reported 50-60x basis-generation speedup excludes one-time training costs (20-150 minutes per NO, three NOs, and extensive hyperparameter search) as well as the GMsFEM eigenproblem cost for generating training targets. The amortized total cost is not analyzed.

The abstract/introduction claim of approximately 60% error reduction relative to standalone NOs is not supported by Table 4; the actual reductions are closer to 31-42% across the reported settings, so the main quantitative claim is overstated.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported, and the appendix admits that cross-validation was not performed because of time constraints. This makes robustness and sensitivity to initialization or hyperparameters unclear.
Code and data are not released, and reproducibility is limited to textual descriptions. For a methods paper in this area, lack of an anonymized code/data artifact weakens verifiability.

The projection regularization term in SAL-PR produces nearly identical results to SAL, so its intended contribution is not demonstrated. The paper does not analyze when or why projection regularization would matter.

There is no theoretical analysis of the subspace loss, convergence, or how errors in the predicted subspace propagate through the coarse-scale solve; therefore, it is unclear whether the learned subspace preserves GMsFEM approximation guarantees.

Baseline comparisons are limited: only standalone FFNO and classical GMsFEM are compared. Other multiscale neural operators, DeepONet variants, PINN-style solvers, or existing ML-augmented GMsFEM approaches are not evaluated.

The full/half/corner subdomain categorization and rotation-based preprocessing may be brittle and are not grid-agnostic; this limits applicability to more general meshes and geometries, as the authors acknowledge but do not resolve.

strengths: The paper targets an important and challenging problem: high-contrast multiscale PDEs where standard neural operators struggle.
The hybrid idea of using a neural operator to accelerate the offline basis construction of GMsFEM is reasonable and could be practically useful.
The proposed subspace alignment loss is a sensible way to handle the non-uniqueness of basis functions and to compare learned subspaces rather than individual basis functions.
The empirical results show a clear speedup in basis generation time relative to classical GMsFEM and improved robustness to changes in the forcing term compared with a standalone neural operator.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental: prior work already used neural networks to predict GMsFEM basis functions, and the proposed subspace alignment loss is essentially a standard principal-angle/subspace overlap measure. The contribution is not a major conceptual advance for a top-tier AI conference.

The abstract and introduction overclaim the error reduction: they state approximately 60% error reduction versus standalone NOs, but Table 4 shows relative L2 reductions of roughly 31-42% (1.7x, 1.6x, etc.), not 60%. This is a serious mismatch between claims and evidence.

The reported 50-60x speedup for basis construction is incomplete and potentially misleading. It ignores the substantial offline training cost (20-150 minutes per neural operator, with three separate NOs) and the expensive GMsFEM data generation for 800 training coefficients. The speedup is only amortized after many queries, which is not discussed or demonstrated for realistic workloads.

The evaluation is narrow: only two time-independent PDEs, one 2D structured grid, 100x100 fine resolution, a 5x5 coarse grid, and a small dataset. There are no experiments on time-dependent problems, irregular domains, 3D, or finer grids, despite these being important for assessing practical impact.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported. Many improvements over GMsFEM are tiny (e.g., 2.49% vs. 2.39% L2) and may be noise; the claim that GMsFEM-NO is 'marginally better' than GMsFEM is not adequately supported.

The baseline comparison is weak. Standalone NO performance is reported only for a FFNO variant, without comparisons to other neural operator architectures, multiscale ML methods, or stronger baselines. It is unclear whether the standalone NO was tuned as thoroughly as the proposed method.

The claimed independence from forcing terms and boundary conditions is largely inherited from GMsFEM rather than being a novel property of the proposed method. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this from the existing GMsFEM framework.
The projection regularization term in the SAL-PR loss yields essentially no improvement over SAL, and the paper offers no compelling explanation or deeper analysis of whether it is useful.

There is no theoretical analysis or guarantee of the quality of the learned subspaces, nor any formal connection between subspace alignment and coarse-scale solution accuracy. The method is evaluated purely empirically, without insight into when or why it should work.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or data are provided at submission time, and the appendix contains duplicated or confusing hyperparameter tables. The claims would be stronger with released code and clearly documented experimental protocols.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel hybrid approach that combines neural operators with GMsFEM by predicting local subspaces rather than individual basis functions, which is a reasonable direction for accelerating multiscale PDE solvers.

The subspace-informed losses (SAL and SAL-PR) are a clear technical contribution; they align predicted and target subspaces geometrically and empirically improve over the per-basis RBFL2 loss in Table 1.
The method achieves substantial inference-time speedup for basis construction (roughly 50-60x over GMsFEM offline in Table 3) and improves over a standalone FFNO baseline on two PDE benchmarks.

The approach is evaluated on both a linear high-contrast diffusion problem and the nonlinear steady-state Richards equation, including an out-of-distribution forcing-term study where standalone NOs fail badly.
Once trained, the basis-prediction stage is independent of the right-hand side, which is a practically useful property for many-query PDE settings.
The paper provides training details, hyperparameters, and compute resources in the appendix, and it acknowledges several limitations in the conclusion.
The problem motivation is clear, and the figures effectively illustrate the GMsFEM-NO pipeline and subdomain handling.
weaknesses: The abstract claims approximately 60% error reduction compared with standalone NOs, but Table 4 shows reductions of roughly 31-42% (a factor of up to 1.7x), so the headline claim is overstated.
Accuracy improvements over classical GMsFEM in Table 2 are marginal (e.g., 2.49% vs 2.39%, 1.15% vs 1.06%), meaning the main practical benefit is speed rather than better solution quality.

The NO training cost (20-150 minutes per NO, with three NOs needed) is not compared against GMsFEM offline cost to establish a break-even point; the reported speedup is only per-sample inference after training.

Experiments are limited in scale: 100x100 grids, 5x5 coarse grids, 1000 samples, and only two time-independent PDEs. This may not demonstrate competitiveness on realistic large-scale multiscale problems.
The claim that the solver is independent of boundary conditions is not empirically supported: only zero Dirichlet boundary conditions are tested, and no boundary-condition variation is evaluated.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported; the results appear to come from a single split and hyperparameter search, making it difficult to assess robustness.

Baselines are narrow: only FFNO and GMsFEM are compared. Other neural operators (FNO, DeepONet, etc.), other multiscale ML methods, and the closely related Spiridonov et al. (2025) approach are not benchmarked.
Code and data are not released, and no anonymized repository is provided, so reproducibility is incomplete despite the appendix details.
There is no theoretical analysis or error bound for the subspace-informed losses; claims about global structural coherence and reduced redundancy are largely speculative.
The projection regularization term SAL-PR yields essentially identical results to SAL, yet it is presented as a contribution; the sensitivity to the hyperparameter lambda is not studied.
The paper contains technical/reference issues: Eq. (6) appears to have malformed LaTeX braces, and the reference list includes errors such as 'Kivakul et al. (2021)' and 'Em Karniadakis'.
The out-of-distribution evaluation only varies the right-hand side forcing; robustness to unseen coefficient fields, boundary conditions, or geometries is not tested.

strengths: Proposes a practical hybrid framework that uses neural operators to predict GMsFEM local spectral basis subspaces, preserving the numerical structure of GMsFEM and making the resulting solver independent of the forcing term.

Introduces subspace-informed losses (SAL and SAL-PR) motivated by Grassmannian geometry and projection consistency, with robustness to basis sign and rotation; these losses outperform the conventional RBFL2 loss in experiments.

Reports strong empirical results: near-GMsFEM accuracy on 2D/3D high-contrast diffusion and nonlinear Richards equation benchmarks, over 60x speedup in basis generation, better OOD forcing performance than standalone NOs, and data efficiency.

Includes comparisons against several relevant baselines, including F-FNO, GNOT, Transolver++, POD-based methods, PCANet, kernel methods, and DeepPOD, with hyperparameter sweeps detailed in appendices.
Demonstrates desirable properties such as resolution invariance (train low, test high), RHS independence, and applicability to time-dependent and mixed-boundary-condition problems in 2D.
Provides substantial appendix material on data generation, training protocols, spectral problem definitions, and additional computational timing analyses.
The core idea—accelerating the costly offline GMsFEM stage with learned local basis predictors—is well motivated and potentially useful for multi-query multiscale PDE simulations.
weaknesses: The breakeven and timing analysis in Appendix N is inconsistent and unreliable: Table 16 reports negative breakeven values (e.g., x = -159 for 100^3) while the text claims positive low breakeven points (159 samples), and the derivation appears to omit or mishandle training-data generation costs. This undermines the central efficiency claim.

Reproducibility is limited: the code is only promised to be made available, not provided; full training data generation and training times are not integrated into the main speedup claims, which focus only on offline basis generation time.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work on ML-assisted multiscale basis construction and reduced-order modeling; the subspace loss is useful but not a major technical leap, and the positioning against methods such as Spiridonov et al. is not fully convincing.

The theoretical claims are incomplete: Appendix C sketches a Grassmannian-distance interpretation and an error bound, but the paper explicitly notes that key questions connecting subspace alignment to final solution error remain for future work, so the claimed rigorous numerical analysis foundation is not fully delivered.

Evaluation gaps exist: standalone NO comparisons are mainly shown on a single 250×250 2D setting; 3D comparisons are limited to GMsFEM vs GMsFEM-NO; the largest 3D case uses only 150 training samples; and statistical significance of small differences is not analyzed.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: for Diffusion with Nbf=8, F-FNO achieves slightly lower error than GMsFEM-NO, and GMsFEM-NO occasionally differs from GMsFEM in either direction without clear explanation beyond statistical variation.
The method trains separate neural operators for each local domain type, which adds engineering complexity and may complicate scaling to more general meshes or domains.

The practical scope is limited: the approach currently requires structured grids, focuses mainly on steady-state Dirichlet problems, and leaves irregular domains, finer grids, and broader PDE classes for future work.
The main paper relies heavily on appendices for baseline results and important analyses, reducing the visibility of the machine-learning contribution for a top-tier AI audience.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: accelerating the costly offline stage of GMsFEM for high-contrast multiscale PDEs.
The hybrid idea of learning GMsFEM basis subspaces with neural operators is sensible, and the group-specific training by local-domain geometry is a practical implementation choice.
The subspace alignment loss is well motivated and empirically improves over the naive relative L2 basis loss in the reported loss-function comparisons.
The experimental evaluation covers 2D/3D diffusion and Richards equation, multiple resolutions, standalone NO baselines, and some reduced-order/hybrid baselines.
The paper demonstrates potentially useful properties such as right-hand-side independence, data efficiency relative to standalone F-FNO, and some resolution transfer.
The reported basis-generation speedup over traditional GMsFEM is large in the offline basis construction step.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: using neural networks to predict or accelerate multiscale basis functions has been explored before, and the proposed subspace/Grassmannian alignment loss is closely related to standard subspace-learning and projector-based losses. The contribution feels incremental.

The theoretical support is weak. Appendix C does not provide a rigorous bound connecting SAL to the final solution error; the displayed error decomposition compares coefficients from different bases in an unjustified way, and the energy-norm issue is acknowledged but not resolved.

The efficiency claims are seriously undermined by Appendix N. The breakeven table reports negative sample counts, which are nonsensical, and the main text's 60x speedup ignores training-data generation and model training costs, which appear to be tens of hours.

The evaluation does not directly compare against the most relevant existing GMsFEM+ML approaches, e.g., Spiridonov et al. (2025), and the claim of superiority over 'other hybrid methods' is therefore not fully supported.
GMsFEM-NO is not consistently better than standalone NOs: in Table 7 it is slightly worse than F-FNO on Diffusion, RHS 8, and improvements appear mainly on more complex forcing terms.

The resolution-invariance claim is overstated: training on 100x100 and testing on 500x500 yields large degradation for Richards equation (e.g., 4.70% vs. 1.93% for GMsFEM), not merely 'minimal loss of accuracy'.
The SAL-PR regularization gives only marginal or inconsistent gains in many settings. The key hyperparameter lambda and its sensitivity are not clearly reported or ablated.
Ablations are insufficient: there is no clear ablation for the domain-type grouping, the number of local basis functions beyond 4 and 8, or the subspace dimension on final accuracy.

Some claims in the abstract and conclusion are stronger than the evidence, including 'reduction in solution error compared to standalone NOs' despite counterexamples, and 'foundation in rigorous numerical analysis' despite the incomplete theory.
The manuscript has clarity and presentation issues, including inconsistent notation around the restriction matrix, typographical errors, and unclear accounting of computational cost.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated hybrid framework that combines GMsFEM with neural operators to accelerate the costly offline basis construction stage.
Introduces subspace-informed losses (SAL and SAL-PR) with a theoretical connection to Grassmannian distance; these outperform the conventional RBFL2 loss and improve solution accuracy.

Strong empirical results: >60x speedup in basis generation, accuracy comparable to GMsFEM, and better robustness than standalone NOs under high-contrast coefficients and out-of-distribution forcing terms.
Thorough evaluation across 2D/3D benchmarks, diffusion and Richards equations, time-dependent problems, mixed boundary conditions, data efficiency, and resolution invariance.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, architecture choices, optimization settings, and a promise to release source code.
Limitations and future work are discussed, including structured-grid restriction and extension to irregular domains.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines existing GMsFEM and FNO architectures, and the subspace alignment loss is closely related to known Grassmannian principal-angle metrics.
Evaluation is limited to structured grids and moderate grid sizes; the largest 3D case uses only 150 training samples, which may not fully demonstrate scalability.

The breakeven analysis in Appendix N contains a sign error: reported negative sample counts contradict the stated formula; corrected values are positive (hundreds to thousands), which affects practical efficiency claims.
Baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: GMsFEM-NO predicts local basis functions and uses the GMsFEM online solver, while standalone NOs learn the full solution operator directly.
Claims of universal superiority over standalone NOs are slightly overstated; e.g., F-FNO achieves lower error on simple diffusion with sufficient training data (Diffusion,8).
Theoretical error bound in Appendix C is informal and does not rigorously link subspace alignment to final solution error in the energy norm.
